newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soy ends down on rationing ideas, technicals.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soy ends down on rationing ideas, technicals.

text.p: CBOT soybeans ended down nearly the 30-cent per bushel limit on Friday, shrugging off USDA's cut in 1996-97 ending stocks and focusing instead on indications high prices had rationed demand, traders said.
Chartists also pointed to negative technical signals that suggested a bearish trend was in place.
USDA on Friday put ending stocks at 125 million bushels, below trade expectations and the lowest in 20 years.
But the market quickly shrugged off the 15 million bushel cut, soying the domestic market was already showing signs of rationing demand.

Floor sources pointed to the National Oilseed Processors Association weekly crush report which showed 25.94 million bushels of soybeans were crushed, one million bushels below trade expectations and the lowest since the October 10 report.

"This report is based on March 1 conditions," a trader said. "It's April 11. We've seen a significant reduction in the crush in the last three weeks, you've had reduction of demand from Taiwan and Europe because of (hog) disease."
Soybeans ended 24-3/4 cents to 1/2 cent per bushel lower with May down 24-3/4 at $8.30-1/2 and new crop November down 2-3/4 at $7.02.

The trader was referring to an outbreak of foot and mouth disease in Taiwan that was expected to cut Taiwan's feed imports. A swine fever epidemic in the Netherlands could cut Europe's imports as well, the trader said.

Trade sources also pointed to vague rumors a commercial firm was bringing more South American soybeans to the U.S. Gulf. Neither Brazilian nor U.S. sources could confirm the rumor and several CBOT traders discounted it.
"There were rumors of commercials bringing beans to the Gulf out of Brazil but our people couldn't confirm anything," a floor source said.
Chartists said the market had been giving off bearish signals since last Friday's limit losses. They said sell orders cropped up early amid ideas the market was due to turn.
"The technicians don't like the bean market any more," a trader said. "They've had signals since Friday that it was getting toppy."
Funds were aggressive sellers of at least 15 million bushels of soybeans on the day and floor sources said they were keying off technical signs rather than fundamental news.

On the day, Refco Inc sold at least three million bushels July and four million May but purchased five million July pit sources said. Cargill Inc and LFG each sold five million July and Smith Barney sold four million July.

In options trade, Smith Barney bought 2,000 May $8.25 puts at 5-1/2 to six cents, LIT America sold 500 May $9.50 calls at 1/2 cent and CIS bought 400 May $7.75 puts at 3/8 of a cent and 100 May $8.25 puts at four cents, traders said.
Soybean volume was estimated by CBOT at 83,000 contracts, compared with Thursday's volume of 52,540.
